en: The Sixth [Section], Explaining Expedient Means, as spoken by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai during the Sui Dynasty and recorded by his disciple Guanding.
"Expedient means" (upāya) is named "skillfulness. It refers to skillful cultivation.
By means of even a minute root of goodness,
one can cause immeasurable practices to reach completion, leading to liberation and entry into the stage of a bodhisattva.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
The meaning is this: that one can, through even a small amount of giving and a small amount of precept-keeping, surpass the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, "expedient means" (upāya) refers to the harmonious convergence of various conditions.
Because it can harmonize and synthesize causes,
and can also harmonize and synthesize the attainment of results.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:
The body of the Tathāgata does not arise from a single cause or a single condition;
rather, the body of the Tathāgata arises from immeasurable merits.
It is to manifest this skillful capacity that the treatise explains the means (upāya).
If one follows the gradual approach, there are four kinds of skillful means (*upāya*).
Each skillful means has its own degree of proximity or distance;
as clarified in the Abhidharma, the five methods of settling the mind (*pañca-viśuddhi-citta*) are considered "distant."
The four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśalamūla*) are proximate;
the general and specific skillful means (*upāya*) may be understood by analogy.
In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), the stages such as the five grades of the provisional name (*jiaming*) and the stage of contemplative practice (*guanxing*) are still far removed from the Truth.
The distant preparatory stage is so named;
the six sense organs being pure and resembling the proximity to reality is called the near preparatory stage.
Now, prior to the five stages, within the provisional designations of the positions,
we further discuss the distant and the near:
twenty-five dharmas constitute the distant preparatory means.
The ten kinds of objects serve as the proximate means.
Transversely and vertically encompassing all, the ten contemplations are complete;
thus one establishes the stage of contemplative practice, capable of giving rise to both the true and the semblance [realizations].
This is called the proximate preparation (*āsannopāya*).
Now, the remote preparation (*dūropāya*) will be explained briefly in five parts.
First, the possession of the five conditions (*pañcapratyaya-samanvāgama*).
Second, rebuking the five desires;
third, abandoning the five hindrances;
fourth, regulating the five matters.
The Five Elements and the Five Dharmas.
Now, the Way does not operate in isolation; its propagation depends upon people.
When people propagate the supreme Dharma, they rely on conditions to advance along the Path.
Therefore, one must possess five conditions.
Once these conditions are fulfilled, one should sever all cravings;
having cleared away external screens of craving, one should purify the mind within.
If the mind is thus tranquil, one should practice the five adjustments.
Once these five matters are adjusted, one should practice the five dharmas;
then one will surely reach the destination.
For example, when a potter wishes to produce vessels,
he first selects a good location—
one free of sand and salt flats, and abundant in grass and water— and there he establishes his workshop.
Next, one must cease other peripheral activities.
If peripheral activities are not stilled, how can one achieve success?
Even if external conditions are ceased, if there is illness within the body, how can one perform tasks?
Although the body may be healthy and strong, if the potter’s wheel is not properly adjusted, it will not produce a vessel.

Likewise, although the superior conditions may be complete, if one does not apply oneself single-mindedly to the task, the work will be abandoned and fail to continue; thus, there will never be any accomplishment.
The five conditions for *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are likewise thus.
A body subject to dependence must rely upon material support, just as one requires a favorable location.
To revile and loathe worldly desires is like severing external conditions.
Abandoning the five hindrances is like treating an internal illness;
harmonizing the five factors is like learning to balance a wheel;
practicing the five dharmas is like performing a task without negligence.
In worldly matters of little significance, causes and conditions must coincide for things to happen;
how much more so for the supramundane Way?
Without a preliminary guide, how could it be easily ascended?
Therefore, one sequentially contemplates twenty-five factors by way of their objective phenomena as a practice of observation (*vipaśyanā*).

Because this tames the coarse and enters the subtle, examining the distracted and bringing it to stillness, it serves as the remote preparatory means (*pūrvaprayoga*) for calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
These five factors and three categories are extracted from the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
One type is from the *Chanyanjing* (Sutra on the Stages of Meditation);
one is established by various Chan masters;
and one consists of those who possess the five conditions.
First, purity of ethical discipline;
second, sufficiency of clothing and food;
third, dwelling in a secluded and quiet place.
Fourth, one ceases all worldly affairs and obligations.
Fifth, one obtains virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
The *Dhyāna-sūtra* states:
Although the four conditions are fully present, it is through the guidance of a good teacher that one proceeds;
therefore, five dharmas are employed as the steps for entering the Path.
If even one is lacking, it will obstruct the task.
An explanation of this is provided in full according to the *Cidi Chanmen* (The Gate to Successive Dhyānas).
Within this, the purity of maintaining the precepts is clarified through four points.
First, the enumeration of the precepts;
second, the explanation of observing the precepts;
third, the explanation of violating the precepts.
Regarding the fourth, the purification through repentance (*sānti*):
as for the enumeration of names,
the sources from which they appear in the sūtras and śāstras are very numerous.
Furthermore, according to the *Śāstra*, there are ten kinds of precepts,
namely: those that are unimpaired and those that are unbroken.
Not pierced;
not mixed;
following the Path.
Unattached,
praised by the wise,
and sovereign.
According to the meditative concentration,
these ten are fully perfected; they take the universal moral precepts as their foundation.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*) consist of the eight types of ethical conduct of body and speech—
namely, the three of the body and the four of the speech— with the addition of abstaining from intoxicants."
This is the pure livelihood of guarding the mental faculty.
It is also said:
the ten wholesome actions constitute śīla.
Even when a Buddha does not appear in the world, these are always present;
therefore, they are called "ancient precepts.
Even ordinary persons cultivate the eight dhyānas when a Buddha does not appear in the world.
Therefore, it is called "old concentration.
The sixty-two types of heterodox views and so forth, as well as the milk-medicine of the old physicians, are called "old wisdom.
As is commonly said:
The statement that "only the eight dhyānas are non-contentious, non-outflow,
and leading" is now challenged: by this same logic,
the ten wholesome paths of action should also be non-outflow and leading.
Since both precepts and wisdom possess adventitious dharmas,
why should meditative concentration alone be without them?
Now, one employs the Three Refuges, the Five Precepts, and the two hundred and fifty [monastic rules].
Regarding the precepts for guests:
as for those who receive the precepts through the ten fundamental methods,
there is, for example, the "Come, Bhikṣu" [ordination], which the Buddha himself spoke of.
One naturally attains the full precepts (upasampadā),
such as Mahākāśyapa who attained the full precepts through his own vow,
or Kauṇḍinya who received the full precepts by seeing the Truths (satyadarśana).
For example, the bhikṣuṇī Prajāpatī received full ordination through the eight rules of respect;
likewise, the bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā received full ordination by sending a messenger.
As the śrāmaṇera Sudāya received full ordination through a discourse on the Dharma;
as the bhikṣu Yaśas and others received full ordination by the "Come hither" formula;
and as Bhadrapāla and Laṅkaka received full ordination by means of the three refuges.
For example, in border regions, one receives full ordination from five *vinaya*-masters;
in the central lands, one receives full ordination through the formal procedure of a motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) with ten people present.
This refers to a person who has received the guest-precepts (*ātithi-śīla*).
The fundamental pure meditative concentration is cultivated through refinement and permeation;
it is the adventitious concentration.
The wisdom regarding the Four Noble Truths is the adventitious wisdom.
It exists only when a Buddha has appeared in the world.
As for the precepts of nature (*dharmatā-śīla*),
whether one has formally received them or not, to transgress them constitutes an offense.
Whether one receives [the precepts] or does not receive and uphold them, it is still virtuous; however,
if one receives the precepts and upholds them, merit arises,
whereas by violating them, one incurs transgression.
One does not receive [the fruit of] non-merit;
one does not receive [the fruit of] transgression without sin.
For example, there is the sin of cutting grass or harming livestock.
The same applies to confession before another person;
both offenses are extinguished.
The *Mahā-śāstra* commentary explains:
"Although the violation of the unmanifested offense (*avijñapti-pāpa*) is equally extinguished, the obligation to repay the life remains.
Thus, one knows that the precepts received through formal undertaking differ from the natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*)."
Therefore, the *Caturvargika-praśna-vinaya* asks regarding the obstructing dharmas:
"Have you not committed a pārājika offense?
A pārājika offense is precisely a transgression of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).
This applies even to the upāsaka precepts,
let alone the great precepts;
provided that one's natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*) are pure.
This is the root of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) and the primary cause for liberation;
based on this intrinsic morality (*prakṛti-śīla*),
one obtains the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) precepts through formal undertaking.
In the Hinayana, the meaning of the unconditioned precepts (*asaṃskṛta-śīla*) constitutes the third aggregate.
In the Mahayana, the *Dharmabherī-sūtra* explains that there are only form and mind, and no third aggregate.
Because the mind is inexhaustible, the precepts are also inexhaustible.
If one considers them from the perspective of the *vinaya* precepts of restraint,
it can be understood that they are characterized by non-action (*avijñapti*).
The precept concurrent with meditative concentration (dhyāna-samvara) arises simultaneously with the concentration itself and has no separate agent.
Some say that it exists at the time of entering concentration but does not exist at the time of emerging from concentration.
Some say that non-manifest action (avijñapti) depends on meditative concentration (samādhi);
as long as the concentration persists, it is not lost.
"Retreat from concentration" means to depart [from it].
Regarding "the non-informative [action] co-existent with the Path," this non-informative [action] depends upon the Path.
Because the Path is without loss, this precept is also without loss.
Since it is common to both the precepts and meditative concentration within the Path,
it is designated by the general name "precept."
Generally, the precepts take the natural precepts (prakṛti-śīla) as their foundation;
thus, a sutra says:
"Depending upon and because of these precepts..."
It is capable of producing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and the wisdom that extinguishes suffering;
this is precisely what is meant here.
II. Explaining the Retainer.
These ten kinds of precepts encompass all precepts.
Regarding the precept that is without deficiency:
this refers to upholding the natural precepts (prakṛti-śīla), including even the four grave offenses (caturmahāpatti).
One should maintain purity and guard [the precepts] as one would a precious, radiant pearl.
Should one violate them,
it is like a vessel that has been broken and is no longer fit for use.
Those on the periphery of the Buddha-dharma are not śramaṇas or sons of the Śākya;
because they have lost the dharma of a bhikṣu, they are termed "deficient.
As for those who do not break [the precepts]:
This refers to upholding the thirteen [precepts].
Because there is no breach or damage, they are called "unbroken.
If one should violate them:
It is like a vessel that has broken.
That which is not pierced refers to the *pāyattika* (pācittiya) and other such offenses.
If one violates [the precepts], it is like a vessel that is pierced and leaking;
because one cannot receive the Way, it is called "pierced.
As for "unmixed":
This refers to maintaining the precepts concurrent with meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Although one maintains the code of discipline (*vinaya*), if one brings to mind thoughts of breaking the precepts,
it is termed "mixed."
Because the mind is sustained by meditative concentration (*samādhi*) such that discursive thoughts do not arise,
it is called "unmixed.
As the Mahāyāna Sūtra says:
Although he did not physically join with that woman,
they conversed and engaged in flirtatious banter;
outside the wall, the sound of bracelets was heard as men and women were seen pursuing one another.
All of these defile the pure precepts.
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* states:
"Although these matters have been prohibited..."
Yet they cause women to wash, wipe, massage,
or speak and gaze at them with lustful minds;
or they observe the precepts for a limited number of days.
Whether one aspires for wealth and pleasure in future lives or for self-indulgence in the heavens,
all such [motivations] are termed impure;
this is not the case if one maintains the unadulterated precepts.
There are none of these thoughts at all.
To "follow the Path" means to accord with the principle of the Truths (satya) and thereby be able to destroy the delusions of views (dṛṣṭi-kleśa).
The precept of non-attachment means that upon seeing the truth and becoming a noble one,
one is no longer stained by or attached to the delusions of conceptual thought.
These two precepts pertain to the observance of the precepts according to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
As for the precepts praised by wisdom and the precepts of mastery,
these pertain to the Bodhisattva’s transformation of others.
Being praised by the Buddha and attaining mastery within the world—
this refers to the observance of the precepts according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
In accordance with meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one fulfills both types of precepts.
This is precisely to follow the Śūraṅgama Samādhi:
without arising from the samādhi of cessation,
to manifest various modes of deportment and display the forms of the ten dharma realms to guide and benefit sentient beings.
Although one’s deportment and movements arise spontaneously, they are always tranquil;
therefore, it is called the "precept of falling into meditative concentration" (*samāhita-śīla*).
The aforementioned various precepts and disciplines serve as preventive restraints.
Therefore, it is called "incomplete.
The precepts of the Middle Way lack no precept;
therefore, they are called "complete."
This is the upholding of the precepts of the ultimate truth of the Middle Way.
By employing the wisdom of the Middle Way, one universally enters into all phenomena.
Thus, the Sūtra says:
Śikṣā. Śikṣā is the name for Mahāyāna precepts.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* elucidates the fivefold precepts as well as the ten kinds of precepts.
The underlying principles and their implications are largely the same.
Even if various sutras and treatises further clarify the characteristics of the precepts,
they ultimately do not go beyond these ten categories.
The three types of precepts mentioned above are called the *vinaya-śīla* (precepts of discipline).
They consist of upholding the good and preventing evil;
from their initial foundation down to the finest detail, they remain untorn and utterly pure.
This collection is called the *vinaya-śīla* (precepts of restraint).
Even ordinary persons with distracted minds are able to maintain and obtain these precepts.
Next is the "precept of non-intermixture."
The mind is sustained by the concentration of the dharma and does not move erratically;
body and speech are likewise tranquil, and the three karmas are as clear as a mirror.
This is the precept concomitant with concentration (*samādhi-saṃvara*).
When entering meditative absorption, it occurs spontaneously and without distraction;
upon emerging from absorption, the body and speech remain supple and likewise undisturbed.
Ordinary persons are able to maintain this when they enter absorption.
The precepts of following the Path pertain to those who have attained the first fruit; having seen the truths and realized the genuine, they become sages.
These are held by sages and cannot be maintained by ordinary worldlings.
The precepts of non-attachment are held by those who have attained the [remaining] three fruits.
Nor is it something maintained by those who have attained only the first fruit.
Wisdom praises its mastery;
this precept must indeed be maintained by Bodhisattvas for the sake of benefiting others.
This is not that which is maintained by those of the Two Vehicles;
it is maintained by those of great root-nature who are fully endowed with meditative concentration.
This is not something that can be maintained even by Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching who practice the six perfections,
let alone by ordinary beings or those of the Two Vehicles.
Previously, I have distinguished the levels of rank and the differing meanings of the various stages.
Regarding the contemplation of principle through the observation of the mind, one who upholds the precepts is fully capable of maintaining the aforementioned ten precepts.
First, the ten precepts are condensed into four intentions;
these are the first four precepts.
However, phenomena produced by causes and conditions serve as the universal object for contemplation;
this refers next to the two precepts.
This means that observing the dharma of dependent origination is itself emptiness;
this contemplation of emptiness constitutes the observance of the precepts.
Next are the two precepts.
Contemplating causes and conditions is itself the provisional;
the provisional contemplation is the observance of the precepts.
Next are the two precepts.
To contemplate phenomena arising from causes and conditions is itself the Middle Way;
this is the Middle Way observation of the precepts.
As for what is called contemplating the mind as a phenomenon arising from causes and conditions: if one contemplates that even a single thought-moment arises from adverse conditions.
It is thus able to destroy the root precepts,
even down to the unadulterated precepts;
because it is contrary to the wholesome, it is called "evil."
Now, by means of a mind of wholesome compliance, one restrains the evil mind;
this enables the fundamental precepts, up to those that are "unmixed" and so forth,
to be accomplished through wholesome compliance and remain free from impairment.
Therefore, it is said that a wholesome mind is called "prevention," and when the unwholesome mind has ceased, the body and speech follow suit.
"Prevention" (fang) is precisely the cessation of evil;
"conformity" (shun) is the practice of goodness.
The practice of wholesome conduct is contemplation (*vipaśyanā*),
and the stilling of wholesome conduct is tranquility (*śamatha*).
This is called maintaining the fourfold precepts by means of the mind produced through the causal conditions of contemplation.
Next, regarding the observation that the mind produced by the causes and conditions of good and evil is itself empty:
as the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* states,
"If one perceives the characteristics of dharmas..."
To be attached to the notions of a self, a person, a sentient being,
or a life-span; likewise, to perceive the characteristics of non-dharmas is also to be attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.
One does not perceive the mark of dharmas, nor does one perceive the mark of non-dharmas.
As it is said in the Parable of the Raft:
"Even dharmas should be relinquished, let alone non-dharmas."
Therefore, one knows that both dharma and non-dharma are equally empty and quiescent;
this is what is called upholding the precepts.
As for what is now called "dharma":
This refers merely to the phenomena of the provisional and the real regarding the two minds of good and evil.
If one perceives the existence of the provisional names "good" and "evil," this constitutes attachment to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
If one perceives the real dharmas of good and evil,
this is likewise attachment to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
What is called the characteristic of non-dharmas is as follows:
If one views the provisional designations of good and evil as non-existent,
this is likewise attachment to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
If one views the substantial reality of good and evil as non-existent, [this is likewise attachment].
They are likewise attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span. Why is this?
Because one should not be attached based on the view of non-arising.
Even views arising from the basis of neither existence nor non-existence are all termed attachment to a self,
a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.
One should contemplate that such phenomena, whether dharmas or non-dharmas, are all precisely emptiness.
Because of this contemplation, one is able to accord with the untainted (*anāsrava*) state and prevent the sixty-two views concerning existence and non-existence; therefore,
it is called the "precept that accords with the Path" (*mārgānulomika-śīla*).
If one repeatedly contemplates this meditation until the cultivation of thought becomes mature,
then as one encounters conditions and objects throughout daily life,
all forms and sounds will be immediately realized as emptiness.
This is called the precept of non-attachment.
It prevents the afflictions of thought and skillfully accords with ultimate truth;
this is what is meant by observing that the mind of dependent origination is empty, thereby upholding these two kinds of precepts.
Next, one contemplates that the mind of causes and conditions is itself a provisional construct.
One knows that this mind is neither mind nor mental phenomena,
yet one does not remain permanently stuck in what is neither mind nor mental phenomena.
By means of the skillful methods of the paths of dharma,
one establishes the mind and the dharmas within non-existence,
thereby uprooting all mental factors.
To guide and benefit sentient beings is praised by the wise;
though one may extensively differentiate immeasurable mental phenomena,
they exist only as names, possessing characteristics like empty space.
Not giving rise to attachment or being constrained by delusive appearances is called mastery.
Such is the provisional contemplation.
Preventing ignorance is to accord with conventional truth;
preventing extreme doctrines is to cease following extreme views and instead contemplate them as provisional.
This is the practice of the two precepts through provisional contemplation.
Next, regarding the contemplation that the mind arising from causes and conditions is itself the Middle Way:
one contemplates that the nature of the mind is ultimately quiescent;
the mind is fundamentally neither empty nor provisional.
Because it is not provisional, it is not mundane;
because it is not empty, it is not supramundane.
It is neither the dharma of the noble ones nor the dharma of ordinary beings.
The quiescence of the two extremes is called the nature of the mind.
To be able to contemplate in this way is called the supreme concentration.
When the mind abides in this samādhi, it is the Śūraṅgama;
fundamentally quiescent and immovable,
it simultaneously illuminates the two truths while manifesting all modes of dignified conduct.
In accordance with such concentration, there is nothing that is not fully perfected.
Thus observing the mind prevents the two extremes and the various evils of ignorance,
and skillfully accords with the principle of the single reality of the Middle Way.
The *Fangbian lun* (Treatise on Guarding the Margins) emphasizes *śamatha*, while the *Shunbian lun* (Treatise on Following the Margins) emphasizes *vipaśyanā*.
These names signify maintaining both precepts through the Middle Way.
Thus, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* says:
The name of the precepts is "Supreme Meaning Light" (Diyi-yi-guang) of the Mahāyāna;
it is neither blue, yellow, red, nor white.
The name of the precepts is filiality; filiality is obedience.
Filial piety is the cessation of unwholesome conduct, and obedience is the practice of wholesome conduct.
Regarding such precepts,
what my Teacher recites, I likewise recite.
One should know that the true essence of the precepts is the wondrous contemplation of the Middle Way;
this is the ultimate observance of the precepts in their superior purity.
As the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* explains at length:
If there is neither self nor what belongs to a self,
and one is far removed from all conceptual proliferation such that nothing at all exists,
this is called the supreme śīla.
Therefore, the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra says:
"The nature of sin is not within, nor is it without,
nor is it in between the two."
As his mind is so, so too are his defilements.
One who can act in this way is called one who understands well; such a person is called one who upholds the Vinaya.
This is precisely the meaning intended.
Furthermore, contemplating the mind while upholding the precepts constitutes five names.
Why is this so? For "prevention" is the meaning of *śīla* (morality).
Contemplation is also like this.
The three contemplations are called the "preventers," while the three delusions are called the "prevented.
This meaning of prevention and restraint pervades the entire dharma-realm.
It is not restricted to body and speech, and so forth.
Furthermore, *vinaya* is named "extinction" because it extinguishes all that is improper regarding body and speech;
therefore, the present contemplation of the mind is also called "extinction."
The contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) can extinguish the errors of view and affliction (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*);
the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti*) can extinguish the errors of the sands of *kleśas*;
the contemplation of the Middle (*madhyama*) can extinguish the error of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Thus, this treatise refutes all errors regarding the universal cessation of the dharma-realm;
it does not stop at the seven branches.
Therefore, the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra says:
One should directly eliminate [afflictions] and not disturb the mind;
this is precisely that meaning.
Furthermore, *prātimokṣa* is named for that which protects one in attaining liberation.
Contemplating the mind is likewise so:
if one does not contemplate the principle of the three truths, the three delusions will certainly not be liberated;
if one perceives the three truths, the three delusions will certainly be liberated.
Such liberation is a liberation that pervades the entire dharma-realm;
it does not merely consist in being liberated from the three miserable realms and transcending birth and death.
Furthermore, as for the reciter:
The "darkly holding" (anṛta-dhāraṇa) in the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi Sūtra* refers to this.
Observing the mind now is likewise so.
The names of the three contemplations (trividha-vipaśyanā) serve to express the principle of the three truths (tri-satya).
This is precisely its text:
knowing that names are not names, one investigates the mind and the principles of reality,
contemplating the continuity of phenomena.
When [the teaching] constantly manifests before one and no deluded thoughts arise,
this is called "recitation."
One who recites in this manner recites throughout the entire dharma-realm; it does not stop at eighty recitations.
Furthermore, as for the Vinaya:
Just as one weighs the gravity [of offenses] to distinguish between transgressions and non-transgressions,
so too does one examine the mind to distinguish the coarse,
evil, and heavy dregs of views and afflictions.
Ignorance within the realm is light;
when the dust of the passions and adventitious defilements arise abruptly,
it becomes heavy again.
The fundamental subtlety has already been explained above in the context of the bodhicitta.
To observe the three principles through the three contemplations is not a transgression.
The three delusions obstructing the three principles are termed "transgressions.
The three medicines treat the three illnesses;
their evaluation is unerring, without the slightest deviation.
Furthermore, it is known that there are three grades of the precept of maintaining ritual matters:
the superior grade results in the retribution of rebirth among devas;
the middling grade results in the retribution of rebirth among humans.
Those of inferior grade receive the retribution of an asura;
those who violate the superior [precepts] fall from the heavens; those who violate the middling [precepts] fall from the human realm.
Having committed this transgression, one falls from the asura realm and enters the three evil paths;
these evil paths are further divided into three grades.
Those with light offenses enter the realm of hungry ghosts;
those with middling offenses enter the realm of animals;
and those with grave offenses enter the realm of hell.
The middle grade also has many types;
the upper-middle, middle-middle, lower-middle, and lower-of-the-lower correspond to the four continents.
The upper grade also has many types.
This refers to the fact that the various heavens within the three realms each have their own ranks and orders.
Furthermore, regarding the three categories of the reality-limit precepts— emptiness, the provisional, and the middle—
each likewise possesses the grades of superior, middling, and inferior.
Regarding the three grades of emptiness: the lower grade constitutes the śrāvakas;

Like thieves, poisons, or noxious weeds, they must be swiftly eradicated;

If one conceals their offenses, they are an ignoble person.

As for the remaining practices, one should simply reform by turning toward the Buddha image with a sincere heart.
It is like having an abscess in a hidden place; if it is concealed and neglected rather than treated, one will die.
By this means, one overturns and destroys the mind that conceals transgressions. Fifth, regarding the severing of the continuous mind:
If one decisively severs [afflictions] and establishes [the path],
completing what has been done without creating anything new, this is repentance.
Regarding those who commit an offense again after having already performed repentance:
it is like the secular law, where the first offense may be pardoned,
but a subsequent commission of the same act is considered a grave offense.
When one first enters the path of practice, transgressions are easily extinguished;
once they have become habitual, they are difficult to eliminate.
Having already been able to vomit them up, why would you consume them again?
By this, one overturns and destroys the mind that constantly dwells on evil matters.
Sixth, regarding the arousal of the bodhicitta:
formerly, one’s own safety and security were at the expense of others, causing universal affliction to all objects of experience.
Now, extensively giving rise to universal salvation that pervades the realm of empty space,
one benefits others; by means of this,
one overturns and destroys the malicious intent that arises everywhere.
Seventh, regarding the cultivation of merit to compensate for transgressions:
whereas in the past one committed offenses through the three karmas without regard for day or night,
now one exerts oneself unremittingly with good deeds of body, speech, and mind.
It is not by moving mountains and filling rivers and seas;
rather, it is by overturning and destroying the mind that indulges in the three karmas of transgression.
Eighth, those who protect the True Dharma.
In the past, you yourself destroyed your own roots of goodness and destroyed those of others;

Now, you protect all roots of goodness through skillful means, increasing and expanding them so that they shall never be severed.
It is like the merit of protecting an entire city.
The Śrīmālādevī-sūtra says:
"To guard the True Dharma and to embrace the True Dharma."
This is the foremost.
This overturns and destroys the absence of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*).
Ninth, the mindfulness of the Buddhas of the ten directions:
In the past, I was intimately associated with evil friends and believed their words;
now, I call to mind the Buddhas of the ten directions and contemplate unimpeded compassion as my uninvited friend,
and I call to mind unimpeded wisdom as my great guide.
This overturns and destroys the mind that accords with evil friends.
Tenth, regarding the contemplation of the emptiness of the nature of offenses:
one thoroughly realizes that the minds of greed, hatred, and delusion are all gates of tranquility.
Why is this? When greed and hatred arise, in what place do they abide?
One knows that this greed and hatred abide in deluded mindfulness.
False thoughts abide in inversion;
inversion abides in the view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi);
the view of a self-body abides in the view of a self (ātmadṛṣṭi).
The view of a self has no abiding place;
though one seeks it diligently throughout the ten directions, a self cannot be found.
My own mind is inherently empty, and thus neither sin nor merit has a master.
Profoundly penetrating the characteristics of sin and merit, it universally illumines the ten directions.
Now, this wisdom of emptiness is in accord with the mind;

All minds are gates of quiescence,

this, in turn, dispels the darkness of ignorance.

first, overturning and destroying non-belief,
